title: Embrace Difficulties
coreMove: Audit a hard practice moment for the mechanism that makes it desirable: retrieval, generation, spacing, variation, correction, or recovery.
sourcePressure: This chapter defines desirable difficulty as challenge that strengthens learning, while excluding overload, random confusion, and errors that never get corrected.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer must avoid saying hard is better; the chapter asks what the difficulty makes the learner do.

sourceAnchors.name: Mia Blundetto
sourceAnchors.detail: First lieutenant in the U.S. Marine Corps, billeted to logistics in Okinawa, who went through jump school despite fearing falling and later had to respond during a C130 parachute jump at 1,250 feet.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Mia Blundetto did not need easy jump training when the air went wrong; she needed difficulty that had already taught her what to do.

sourceAnchors.name: Cal Poly baseball contextual-interference study
sourceAnchors.detail: Experienced Cal Poly batters took extra practice under different pitch regimens; random pitches felt harder but built better real hitting than blocks of known pitch types.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A curveball is a different lesson when you do not know it is coming.

sourceAnchors.name: Elizabeth and Robert Bjork desirable-difficulties work
sourceAnchors.detail: The notes cite the Bjorks on making learning hard in a good way and on reloading after delay.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The Bjorks gave a name to the friction that helps because it makes memory reload instead of coast.

hook: Do not open by saying learning is harder than it looks
Do not use a generic desk-and-notes image
Do not start with a broad claim about students today
counterintuition: Do not use the shell easier is not better
Do not flatten the chapter into struggle is good
Do not contrast comfort and growth in generic coaching language
tryThisNow: Do not write set a timer and reflect
Do not ask for a vague study audit
Do not use a reusable close-your-notes prompt without a chapter-specific action
examples: No repeated mug, marker, dosing cup, bike helmet, radiator, bus depot, classroom, or narrow-kitchen shells
No six examples that all start with a timestamp and a named protagonist
No generic student rereads notes scene unless the visible beat changes the method

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective reveal, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: Rachel, an emergency-dispatch trainee handling mixed radio calls
exampleSpecs.audience: public-safety trainees whose drills are either too easy or overwhelming
exampleSpecs.stakes: the first real multi-unit call will expose whether the difficulty trained triage
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the supervisor removes one distraction, keeps two competing calls, and makes Rachel choose the first callback with feedback after the run
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Two radio channels crackle over a dark dispatch console.

exampleSpecs.domain: Thomas, a chess-club coach teaching rook endings
exampleSpecs.audience: coaches who need challenge without drowning beginners
exampleSpecs.stakes: students lose interest if every puzzle is either obvious or impossible
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he hides the engine, gives a position just beyond comfort, lets students generate candidate moves, then replays the correction
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The tournament clock ticks beside three wooden rooks.

exampleSpecs.domain: Juliette, a surgical-tech instructor practicing sterile breaks
exampleSpecs.audience: health-care trainers designing errorful but safe practice
exampleSpecs.stakes: real procedures require noticing and repairing a contamination break quickly
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she stages a low-stakes sterile-field error, waits for the trainee to catch it, then has him reset the field correctly
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 10:06 a.m., Juliette folds one blue drape corner the wrong way.

exampleSpecs.domain: Niklas, a firefighter academy instructor adding smoke to search drills
exampleSpecs.stakes: too much smoke makes the drill blind panic instead of learning
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he asks the recruit to predict the route, adds controlled smoke and one blocked doorway, then debriefs the missed hand sweep
exampleSpecs.firstImage: How much smoke teaches before it erases the room?

exampleSpecs.domain: Catarina, a language tutor using generation before explanation
exampleSpecs.audience: adult learners who want rules before trying
exampleSpecs.stakes: students need to produce a sentence without waiting for the rule to be served first
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she asks for a guessed past-tense sentence, corrects the error, and has the learner say a new sentence with the repair
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Guess first," Catarina says, covering the verb table.

exampleSpecs.domain: Chidi, a robotics mentor preparing students for sensor failure
exampleSpecs.audience: competition teams that overfit to smooth lab runs
exampleSpecs.stakes: the robot will face uneven light and noisy sensors at regionals
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the postmortem identifies which added obstacles forced recovery and which ones merely broke the practice
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Chidi one dead sensor to stop calling every obstacle useful.

skillTargets: judge whether difficulty has a learning mechanism
distinguish corrected errors from abandoned errors
set challenge below overload and above easy fluency

tryThisNowSpec: Name one hard part of your current practice and write the mechanism it serves; if you cannot name one, simplify or redesign it.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
